about: Seventy plants, animals, fish, and fungi you can walk outside and find along the lower end of Five Mile Creek. Every photograph is a real one with a name on it, and most of them were taken in Alabama.

creek.name: Creek
creek.title: Five Mile Creek
creek.desc: The water and everything that lives along its banks. Fish, amphibians, crawdads, and the insects that tell you whether the water is clean.
creek.gear: Waterproof boots or old shoes you do not mind getting wet. A walking stick helps with slippery rocks. Watch your step on algae covered stones, which are about as forgiving as ice.

woods.name: Woods
woods.title: The Bottomland Woods
woods.desc: Hardwood forest along the creek corridor. Deer, fox, turkey, mushrooms, and the things that live under rocks and fallen logs.
woods.gear: Long pants, boots, and gaiters during snake season, March to October. Bring water. Large wild grape vines in the deep woods can be cut for water in an emergency if you know what you are looking for, and the cut vine should drip clear, not milky.

treetops.name: Treetops
treetops.title: The Canopy
treetops.desc: Everything that lives above your head. Hawks, owls, woodpeckers, bats, cicadas, and the ecosystem that exists sixty feet up.
treetops.gear: Binoculars change everything up here. A field guide to the birds of Alabama helps. Early morning is the best time, when the birds are active and calling.

swamp.name: Swamp
swamp.title: The Bottomland Swamp
swamp.desc: Low, wet ground where the creek floods and the water sits. Turtles, snakes, salamanders, and things that thrive in standing water.
swamp.gear: Rubber boots, because you will get wet. Gaiters are essential here rather than optional. Cottonmouths prefer still, swampy water over moving creek water. Watch where you step and where you put your hands.

meadow.name: Meadow
meadow.title: The Fields and Clearings
meadow.desc: Open ground, field edges, and the margins where forest meets clearing. Hawks overhead, deer at the edges, wildflowers, and the mice that feed everything.
meadow.gear: A hat for the sun and light colored clothing so you can spot ticks. Check yourself thoroughly after walking through tall grass. This is where chiggers live, so tuck your pants into your socks.

species.name: Bluegill
species.body: The bluegill, called bream by everyone around here, is the fish most Five Mile Creek kids catch first. Patient, curious, and relentless at stealing bait.

facts.v: Live cricket under a bobber. Red worms and nightcrawler pieces also work. Match whatever is naturally hatching on the water.
Early morning and late afternoon. Spawning in late spring, when males guard shallow gravel nests and will bite anything that comes close.
A long cane pole with no reel is still the best tool on Five Mile Creek. Quiet, accurate, drops a cricket exactly where you want it.

species.otw: A cricket under a bobber on a cane pole. Check any shady hole tight against the bank. The bream is in there and it just needs a reason to commit.

quiz.q: You see a flash of color near a sunken log. Best way to catch a bluegill on Five Mile Creek?
choices: Fly fishing with a dry fly
Cricket under a bobber on a cane pole
quiz.right: That's exactly right.
quiz.wrong: The old-timers knew. A cricket under a bobber on a cane pole.

photos.alt: A bluegill held flat in an open hand above shallow water, showing the dark ear flap and the olive and orange banding along its side.
A bluegill held in two hands and filling the frame, with a blue green sheen along its gill cover.
A small bluegill lying across an open palm above green water with its fins spread.

species.name: Under the Rock
species.body: Turning over a flat rock in a fast riffle is the oldest water quality test there is. What you find tells you everything about the health of Five Mile Creek.

facts.v: Stonefly nymphs, mayfly nymphs, caddisfly larvae in little stick cases. These need clean, well-oxygenated water.
Mostly just worms and midges, which tolerate pollution. Their dominance means the creek is stressed.
Hellgrammites and stonefly nymphs are premium bait. Creek fishermen have known this for centuries: the same creatures that indicate clean water are the ones fish want to eat.

species.otw: Old creek fishermen turned over rocks before choosing where to fish, not for science, but because what they found told them where the fish were feeding.
species.clue: A flat rock in the riffle. Flip it over and see what's living underneath.

photos.alt: A stonefly nymph on a wet rock, flat bodied with long antennae and two tails, the shape that turns up on the underside of a stone in a riffle.
An adult stonefly resting on wet sand with its wings folded flat down its back.
A pale stonefly with folded wings resting on a green fern frond.

species.name: Crawdad
species.body: Crayfish are the cornerstone of the creek food web. Food for bass, bream, herons, and raccoons. Catch them, cook them, use them as bait, or just watch them work.

facts.v: Cup your hand downstream when you lift a rock. Crayfish scoot backward, right into your hand if you are patient and positioned right.
A live crayfish hooked through the tail is one of the best bass baits in any Alabama creek. Let it walk on the bottom naturally.
Boil in heavily salted water with Old Bay for 3 to 5 minutes. Eat the tails. Takes a pile of them but absolutely worth the work.

species.otw: Lower a piece of salt pork on a string into a deep hole, wait, then lift slowly. The crawdad grips so hard it won't let go until it's clear of the water.
species.local: A reliable sign in clean riffles and under flat rocks where the current breaks just enough to make a pocket.
species.clue: Something scooted backward when you lifted that rock.

photos.alt: A pale crayfish underwater beside a rock, claws forward and legs braced against the current.
A crayfish held between finger and thumb, showing the blue and orange banding on its claws and the ridged shell.
Several crayfish crowded together in shallow clear water over gravel.

species.name: Great Blue Heron
species.body: Five Mile Creek's best fisherman. Residents have spotted one regularly working the shallows near the old bridge site. A heron working your stretch of creek means the water has fish.

facts.v: A heron's strike covers 18 inches in about 40 milliseconds. The fish is already caught before you see the heron move.
Fish up to 12 inches, frogs, crayfish, snakes, and occasionally small mammals near the water. They swallow everything whole.
Herons need clean, fish-rich water. Every confirmed sighting on Five Mile Creek is worth writing down. It is real ecological data.

species.otw: Mountain tradition says to watch where a kingfisher dives, and that is where the fish are. The heron gives you the same information with more patience.
species.local: Often spotted working the shallows near bridge approaches and slower bends after rain settles out.

quiz.q: The great blue heron stands motionless for two full minutes, then strikes. What is it doing?
quiz.right: Exactly. Patience is the entire technique.
quiz.wrong: Patience is the whole technique. It waits for the fish to come to it.

photos.alt: A great blue heron standing among lily pads and marsh plants in shallow water.
A great blue heron with its wings spread coming down into a bare tree against blue sky.
A great blue heron standing at the edge of the surf, neck folded, in full side view.

species.name: Mayfly
species.body: Mayflies spend up to a year as aquatic nymphs before emerging as adults for just one or two days, long enough to mate and die. A mayfly hatch on Five Mile Creek is worth seeing.

facts.v: Mayfly nymphs are highly sensitive to low oxygen and pollution. Finding them means the creek is relatively clean at that spot.
When mayflies are hatching, fish feed aggressively at the surface. Match the color and size of what's hatching.
Spring and fall hatches are most dramatic on Alabama creeks. Early morning and evening, especially after a warm rain.

quiz.q: A mayfly spends most of its life in which form?
quiz.right: Right. The adult you see is just the ending.
quiz.wrong: The flying adult is just the finale. Almost the entire life is lived underwater.

photos.alt: A mayfly resting on pale stone with its wings held up over its back and two long tails trailing behind.
A mayfly clinging to a window with its wings raised and three long tails hanging below it.
A mayfly on a white window frame, wings folded up and tails curved back.

species.name: Water Snake
species.ctx: On a rock at the water's edge
species.body: The northern water snake is the most common snake along Five Mile Creek and is almost always mistaken for a cottonmouth. It is not venomous. Please don't kill water snakes.

facts.v: Cottonmouths prefer still, swampy water. They have blocky triangular heads and cat-eye pupils. When uncertain, leave it alone. That is always the right call.
The black rat snake (called "chicken snake" locally) also lives near Five Mile Creek. Non-venomous, excellent climber, important rodent control.
Fish, frogs, crayfish, salamanders. Important predators keeping populations balanced in the creek ecosystem.

species.lookalike: Usually mistaken for a cottonmouth. Along moving water here, a patterned water snake is much more likely. Leave both alone and give them room.
species.local: Most often seen sunning on low branches, roots, or rocks beside the water rather than out in dry upland woods.

quiz.q: You see a thick, patterned snake near Five Mile Creek. It's most likely:
choices: A northern water snake, not venomous
A rat snake that fell in
quiz.right: Correct. Leave it alone and it'll leave you alone.
quiz.wrong: Almost certainly a northern water snake. The cottonmouth is far less common in moving water.

photos.alt: A northern water snake coiled on the bank at the edge of green water with its head resting on its own body.
photos.where: S College St, Auburn, AL, US

photos.alt: A young northern water snake stretched across wet leaves, showing the dark crossbands over its back.
The head of a northern water snake breaking the surface of muddy water as it swims.

species.name: Green Frog
species.body: Green frogs live along the entire length of Five Mile Creek. Amphibians breathe partly through their skin, so they are exquisitely sensitive to water quality and pesticides. A healthy frog population is a very good sign.

facts.v: A plunk like a loose banjo string. That is the male green frog calling from the bank, May through August.
The bullfrog also lives here. Its deep "jug-o-rum" call carries a long way on summer nights.
Frogs absorb chemicals directly through their skin. Pesticide runoff and herbicides hit them harder than almost any other animal.

species.otw: Bullfrog gigging at night with a lantern along the creek bank is still legal in Alabama with a license. Move the lantern slowly so the frog watches the light, not you.
species.lookalike: Green frogs and bullfrogs overlap. Green frogs give the banjo string note and bullfrogs give the deeper jug-o-rum call.
species.clue: Something went "plunk" into the water before you could see it.

photos.alt: A green frog sitting in shallow water among green leaves with only its head and back above the surface.
A green frog on a rock in side view, showing the ridge that runs back from the eye down each side.
A green frog on a wet moss covered bank beside the water.

species.name: Largemouth Bass
species.body: Largemouth bass are the top predator in Five Mile Creek. A healthy bass population means the food web is working. Catch one, look it over, release it.

facts.v: Bass do not patrol open water. They sit against something: an undercut bank, a sunken log, a rock ledge, a depth change. Put your bait there.
Live crayfish or minnows from the creek itself are hard to beat. Match what's naturally in the water.
Most Five Mile Creek bass run 10 to 14 inches. Releasing them healthy keeps the population building. Wet your hands before handling.

species.otw: Find where the creek bends, find where it deepens, find where a tree fell in the water, then fish where all three meet. That's where the big one lives.

quiz.q: You're fishing a deep hole in Five Mile Creek. Where exactly should your bait be?
choices: On the surface near the middle
Right against the undercut bank or submerged log
As deep as possible straight down
quiz.right: That's where the fish lives.
quiz.wrong: Bass are ambush predators and they need structure. Put it against the undercut bank.

photos.alt: A largemouth bass held up by the lower jaw, showing the dark band along its side and a mouth that reaches past the eye.
A small largemouth bass held above the water with the creek and trees behind it.
A largemouth bass held up with its mouth open, dark green over white, against leaves.

species.name: Dragonfly
species.body: Dragonflies are one of the best signs of a healthy creek. Their larvae live underwater for 1 to 3 years before emerging as adults.

facts.v: A single adult dragonfly can eat hundreds of mosquitoes per day. They are one of the most effective natural mosquito controls that exists.
Scientists use dragonfly larvae to measure creek health without expensive equipment. Their absence at a likely site is a red flag.
Twelve-spotted skimmer, blue dasher, and widow skimmer are all common along Five Mile Creek in summer.

quiz.q: A creek full of dragonflies means:
choices: The water is stagnant, because they like still water
The water is relatively clean, because larvae need good oxygen
quiz.right: Right. The larvae underwater tell the real story.
quiz.wrong: Actually the opposite. Dragonfly larvae need clean, well oxygenated water to survive.

photos.alt: A blue dragonfly perched on a bare stem with its wings held out flat and its abdomen raised.
A dragonfly clinging to a stem in bright sun, wings spread and clear, with large compound eyes.
A black winged damselfly with a metallic green body resting on a green leaf.

species.name: Creek Snail
species.body: Freshwater snails are one of the most overlooked indicators of creek health. Alabama has more freshwater snail species than any other state, many of them found nowhere else on earth.

facts.v: Alabama's rivers and creeks contain the highest freshwater snail diversity in North America. Many species are endemic, living in a single creek system and nowhere else.
Snails graze algae from rocks, keeping the creek clean. They're food for fish, crayfish, and turtles. Simple animals doing essential work.
Like mayflies, many snail species require clean, well-oxygenated water. Their presence or absence tells you something real about creek health.
Sedimentation from erosion smothers snail habitat. Every cleared bank that sends dirt into the creek directly impacts these animals.

species.clue: Small spiral shells cling to the rocks in the current.

photos.alt: Two freshwater snail shells on a wet rock, tall and pointed with brown and white banding.
A creek snail held on a fingertip with its dark pointed shell turned to show the opening.
A dark creek snail held between finger and thumb above the gravel of a shallow creek.

species.name: White-tailed Deer
species.ctx: At the forest edge at dawn
species.body: White-tailed deer are the most visible large mammal along the creek. They browse the forest edge at dawn and dusk, and their trails through the bottomland are some of the oldest paths in these woods.

facts.v: Bucks shed antlers every year between January and March. Shed hunting, walking the woods looking for dropped antlers, is a legitimate winter activity. Dogs can be trained to find them.
Alabama deer season runs roughly October through February depending on zone. Check ADCNR for current dates. Archery season opens first.
Heart-shaped hoofprints in creek mud are deer. Two pointed toes close together. A running deer spreads its toes and dew claws show behind the main print.
Deer will eat almost anything in a garden. Fencing is the only reliable deterrent, and they can jump 8 feet, so it needs to be tall or angled.

species.otw: Old-timers tracked deer by reading the browse line. The height where all leaves and twigs are nipped off tells you how many deer are using an area. A low browse line means heavy pressure.

quiz.q: A white-tailed deer raises its tail and flashes white while running. Why?
choices: To signal danger to other deer
To confuse predators with the flash
quiz.right: Right. That white flag is a warning to every other deer watching.
quiz.wrong: The white tail is a danger signal. Every deer that sees it knows to be alert or run.

photos.alt: Two white-tailed deer standing at the edge of a mown field in front of the woods.
A spotted fawn curled up in low green plants with its ears out, staying still.
Three deer out in a green field at the foot of a wooded slope.

species.name: Shed Antlers
species.body: Every buck drops both antlers between January and March. They start growing new ones almost immediately. Finding a shed antler is like finding a piece of the forest's calendar, proof of who was here and when.

facts.v: Late January through March. Walk deer trails, bedding areas, and fence crossings where the jolt of jumping can knock an antler loose.
Decreasing daylight after the rut triggers a hormonal change. A thin layer of bone between antler and skull dissolves, and the antler simply falls off.
Keep it. Shed antlers are legal to collect in Alabama. They make good dog chews, knife handles, or just mantelpiece conversation pieces.
Finding both sides from the same buck is the goal. They usually drop within a hundred yards of each other, but not always.

species.otw: An old deer hunter's trick: find a shed, then circle 50-100 yards in every direction. The other side is usually nearby. The buck didn't go far between losing one and losing the other.
species.clue: Something pale and branching on the ground, half-buried in leaves.

photos.alt: A shed antler lying on winter grass, three points on one beam and the rough burr at the base where it broke away from the skull.
A shed antler lying on snow, its tines curving upward, cast whole from one side of a buck head.

species.name: Chanterelle
species.body: Chanterelles grow in the hardwood bottomland along Five Mile Creek from late spring through fall, especially after summer rain. One of the finest wild edibles in the Alabama forest.

facts.v: Under oaks and hardwoods after summer rain. They grow in the same spots year after year, so find one spot and return to it.
The jack-o-lantern mushroom looks similar but grows in clusters at tree bases, has true gills, and glows faintly in the dark. It will make you very sick.
Sauté in butter with salt. Do not wash them. Brush off debris with a dry brush. Simple is best.

species.otw: Chanterelles are called golden teachers, not for any special property, but because learning to identify them correctly teaches you the patience and careful observation needed for all foraging. Rushing gets you sick.
species.lookalike: The jack-o'lantern mushroom is the dangerous look-alike. Chanterelles have blunt, forking ridges rather than sharp true gills.
species.local: Good years come after warm summer rains when the woods stay damp for a few days in a row.

quiz.q: You find a golden-orange mushroom in the bottomland. How do you confirm it's a chanterelle?
choices: It grows in clusters at a tree base
Forking ridges (not true gills) and apricot scent
It glows faintly in the dark
quiz.right: That is the key. Forking ridges, not gills.
quiz.wrong: The test: forking ridges (not true gills) under the cap, and an apricot scent. The poisonous look-alike has true gills and grows in clusters at trees.

photos.alt: A golden chanterelle on dark leaf litter, its cap wavy at the edge and its ridges running down the stem.
A cluster of chanterelles seen from below, showing the blunt forking ridges that run down the stem instead of true gills.
Two slender yellow chanterelles standing in leaf litter on the forest floor.

species.name: Oyster Mushroom
species.body: Oyster mushrooms grow in overlapping clusters on dead hardwoods along Five Mile Creek, especially in cool, moist weather. One of the easiest wild mushrooms to identify and one of the best to eat.

facts.v: White to tan, shelf-shaped, growing in clusters from dead wood. Gills run down the stem. Mild, pleasant smell. No look-alikes that grow from wood in clusters this way.
Spring and fall are peak season, but oysters fruit in winter too during warm spells. After rain is always the best time to check logs.
Sauté in butter with garlic. They shrink a lot, so cook a generous amount. Outstanding in eggs or on toast.
Oak, sweetgum, and tulip poplar along the creek bottomland are the most productive hosts.

species.otw: Any dead log near water that hasn't been checked in a few days after a rain is worth looking at. Oysters can appear overnight and go fast, because the weather window is short.
species.lookalike: People sometimes confuse oysters with pale shelf fungi, but true oyster mushrooms grow in layered clusters from wood with gills running down the stem.
species.clue: A cluster of shelf mushrooms growing from a dead log near the water.

photos.alt: A cluster of pale oyster mushrooms growing in overlapping shelves out of a moss covered log.
Oyster mushrooms stepping up the side of a standing dead tree in tiers.
A single oyster mushroom seen from below and the side, its gills running down onto a short stem.

species.name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
species.body: Lion's mane is one of the most distinctive wild mushrooms in the Alabama forest: white, cascading, and resembling exactly what its name describes. No look-alikes. When you see it, you know it.

facts.v: Pure white cascading spines growing from a single point on the tree. No cap, no gills, no stem to speak of. Unmistakable. Turns yellow-brown as it ages, so harvest it young.
Mild, with a texture often compared to crab or lobster. Slice thick, sauté in butter until golden. One of the finest wild mushrooms in eastern North America.
Lion's mane has significant research interest for nerve growth support. Whether the amounts in a meal make a difference is debated, but it is worth knowing.
Old oaks and beeches, usually on wounds or branch stubs. Look 8 to 12 feet up as well as at eye level, because it often fruits out of easy reach.

species.otw: The old rule: when you find a lion's mane tree, remember it. Check it the same week every year in late fall. They often fruit from the same wound repeatedly for years.
species.clue: A white cascading mass hanging from a wound in an old hardwood.

photos.alt: A lion's mane mushroom growing from the side of a fallen log, a rounded white mass hanging in soft spines.
A lion's mane mushroom on a log in open woods, white against the bark with its spines hanging below.
A close view of a lion's mane mushroom from underneath, showing the dense white spines that take the place of gills.

species.name: Box Turtle
species.body: The eastern box turtle is one of the most recognizable residents of these bottoms: a domed shell with orange and yellow markings, wandering slowly through the bottomland and forest floor. They can live 50 to 100 years.

facts.v: Box turtles can live longer than most people. The big old one in your yard may have been there since your grandparents' time.
Mushrooms, berries, earthworms, insects, and carrion. They help spread fungal spores and seeds throughout the forest.
Box turtles cross roads slowly and get hit constantly. If you see one in the road, move it to the side it was heading toward, not back where it came from.
Box turtles rarely travel more than a few acres their entire lives. Moving one far from where it was found is effectively a death sentence, because they cannot navigate back.

species.otw: Old-timers kept box turtles in the garden to eat slugs and insects. They'll come back year after year if you leave them be. Do not move them from your property. They will stay if they want to.
species.clue: Something moves slowly through the leaf litter near the bank.

photos.alt: An eastern box turtle on leaf litter in side view, its high domed shell marked with bright yellow lines on dark brown.
A box turtle standing on bare sand with its head out, showing the yellow pattern across the top of the shell.
A box turtle walking across gravel with its domed shell in profile.

species.name: Red Fox
species.ctx: At the edge of the field at dusk
species.body: Red foxes are active along Five Mile Creek's field edges and forest margins, especially at dawn and dusk. You're more likely to hear their bark than see them, a strange raspy scream that sounds like someone being murdered.

facts.v: The red fox bark is one of the more startling sounds of the Alabama night, a sharp raspy WAAAH. Terrifying the first time you hear it in the dark.
Field mice, rabbits, birds, insects, berries, and carrion. Foxes are critical for keeping field mouse populations controlled.
Foxes often reuse groundhog burrows, enlarging them. A large burrow with scattered bones and fur nearby is likely an active fox den.
The gray fox is also present along Five Mile Creek and is the only canid that regularly climbs trees. Smaller and less bold than the red.

species.otw: Old-timers said a fox's track tells its mood. A direct, purposeful line means hunting. A wandering, looping track means it's just moving through. Learning to read tracks is learning to read the land.
species.clue: A flash of red at the edge of the field as the light fades.

photos.alt: A red fox trotting across a mown lawn in full side view, red coat, black legs, and a white tipped brush.
photos.where: Town Creek Park, Auburn, AL, US

photos.alt: A red fox standing on a rock in a grassy clearing, looking straight at the camera.
Two red foxes lying together in the grass at the edge of a field.

species.name: Opossum
species.ctx: On a branch over the water
species.body: The opossum is one of Five Mile Creek's odder residents: slow moving, ancient looking, and deeply misunderstood. They are one of the most ecologically valuable animals in the watershed.

facts.v: A single opossum can consume up to 5,000 ticks per season. They groom compulsively and ingest ticks while doing it. Extraordinary tick control for a neighborhood.
Playing possum is an involuntary response to extreme stress. The animal actually loses consciousness. It can last minutes to hours and it cannot control it.
Opossums are largely immune to most snake venoms, including copperhead and cottonmouth. Researchers are studying their blood for antivenin applications.
Opossums almost never carry rabies, because their body temperature is too low for the virus to survive. One of the safest wild animals to encounter.

species.otw: Old-timers called them "possums" and ate them regularly. Possum and sweet potatoes was a legitimate Appalachian dish, baked together, with the fat from the possum basting the potatoes. Not fashionable now, but it fed families.
species.local: Shows up around sheds, compost edges, and brushy transitions where insects and fallen fruit collect.

quiz.q: The opossum is remarkable for which actual biological trait?
choices: It's the only marsupial native to North America
It can hold its breath underwater for 10 minutes
It has the best night vision of any North American mammal
quiz.right: Right. The only marsupial native to North America.
quiz.wrong: The opossum is the only marsupial native to North America. It raises young in a pouch, like a kangaroo.

photos.alt: An opossum standing on a board at night facing the camera, its pale face and pink nose lit and its pink feet gripping the edge.
A young opossum beside a tree trunk with its ears back and its pink nose forward.
A trail camera frame of an opossum crossing a log in the woods at night.

species.name: Armadillo
species.body: The nine-banded armadillo has expanded throughout Alabama in recent decades. Their leaf-litter rooting is audible from 50 feet away. They have no idea how loud they are.

facts.v: Armadillos expanded north from Texas and Florida through the 20th century, aided by a warmer climate and no natural predators willing to deal with that shell.
Nearly blind. They navigate by smell and can't see you standing still right in front of them. Walk slowly toward one for a memorable experience.
Armadillos always give birth to exactly four identical quadruplets from a single egg. Every time. No exceptions.
Their rooting for beetle larvae and earthworms does minor damage to lawns but is relatively harmless in the bottomland, where they prefer soft, moist soil near water.

species.otw: Armadillos weren't here when the old-timers were young. Their appearance is a living record of climate change. They cannot survive extended freezes, and those have become rarer here.
species.clue: Something is crashing through the leaves, sounding much larger than it is.

photos.alt: A nine-banded armadillo standing on short grass in side view, its banded shell and long ears clearly visible.
photos.where: Nova Friburgo - State of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

photos.alt: An armadillo rooting nose down through tall dry grass.
An armadillo working through fallen leaves and twigs with its armoured back turned to the camera.

species.name: Coyote
species.body: Coyotes have expanded throughout Alabama and are well established along Five Mile Creek. Intelligent, adaptable, and mostly invisible. You will hear them far more than you will see them.

facts.v: Field mice, rabbits, groundhogs, persimmons, berries, carrion, insects. They eat what is available and are genuinely omnivorous.
Similar to a medium dog but in a straight line. Coyotes place their back feet almost exactly where their front feet were, which conserves energy.
Litters born in spring, April to May. Pups begin howling by late summer. The sudden increase in noise in August means a new generation.
Secure your chickens and small pets at night. Don't feed them intentionally or accidentally (unsecured garbage). They do real ecological work keeping rodent populations in check.

species.lookalike: At a distance and in poor light, a coyote reads as a loose dog. The tail is the tell, carried low and straight rather than up.

quiz.q: You hear coyotes howling along Five Mile Creek at night. This means:
choices: The pack is attacking something large
They are communicating, locating each other and marking territory
There's a fire nearby scaring them
They only howl when they're hungry
quiz.right: Right. It is communication, not crisis.
quiz.wrong: Howling is communication. They are talking to each other, not signaling an attack.

photos.alt: A coyote standing at the edge of a clearing at night with its ears up, caught in a light.
photos.where: Cypress Bend Golf Course, Gulf Shores, AL, US

photos.alt: A coyote track pressed into red mud, four toes and a triangular pad, with a boot toe beside it for scale.
A trail camera frame of a coyote walking through woods in the dark.

species.name: Wild Hog
species.body: Wild hogs are an invasive species doing serious damage to Five Mile Creek's watershed. They root up streambanks, destroy native vegetation, and send sediment directly into the water. Not a native species. Not beneficial.

facts.v: A single sounder of hogs can destroy an acre of creek bank overnight. They uproot the vegetation that holds soil in place and filters runoff.
Females can have two litters per year of 4 to 8 piglets each. They are nearly impossible to eliminate once established, and only sustained pressure controls numbers.
Wild hogs are not protected in Alabama. They can be hunted year-round on private land without a license. Hunting them is encouraged.
Rooted-up soil, wallows (muddy depressions near water), fence damage, and tracks with two pointed toes splayed wide.

species.otw: Feral hogs around here were not always a problem. They spread from poorly managed domestic pigs. Old-timers let hogs roam because they'd come home at slaughter time. That practice ended. The hogs didn't.

quiz.q: Wild hogs along Five Mile Creek are a major problem because:
choices: They compete with deer for acorns
They root up the soil and vegetation, causing erosion into the watershed
quiz.right: Exactly right. They destroy the bank and fill the creek with sediment.
quiz.wrong: Rooting is the real damage. They destroy the vegetated bank that filters runoff and holds soil out of the water.

species.name: Striped Bark Scorpion
species.body: Yes, scorpions live along Five Mile Creek. The striped bark scorpion is found throughout Alabama. Small, pale tan, and less dangerous than its reputation.

facts.v: The striped bark scorpion's sting is painful but rarely dangerous to healthy adults, comparable to a bee sting. Children, elderly, and those with allergies should be more careful.
Under loose bark, in wood piles, under rocks at the edge of moist areas. Check your boots if they've been sitting outside overnight.
Insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates. Part of the ground-level predator community keeping insect populations in check.
Scorpions fluoresce bright blue-green under UV/black light. A UV flashlight at night near a log pile is a reliable way to find them.

species.otw: Old-timers in the area called them "stinging lizards" and checked their boots every morning. Good practice.
species.clue: You lift a piece of loose bark from a log near the creek. Something scuttles.

photos.alt: A striped bark scorpion on red sand, pale tan with two dark stripes down its back and a slender tail.
A pale striped bark scorpion on sand, claws forward and tail curled over its back.

species.name: Striped Skunk
species.ctx: At the forest edge at dusk
species.body: Striped skunks are common along Five Mile Creek's forest margins and residential edges. They eat grubs, insects, mice, and eggs. Useful pest controllers that would rather avoid you entirely.

facts.v: Foot-stamping, raised tail, backward shuffling, and sometimes a short charge. If you see any of these, back away slowly. They do not want to spray, because it costs them energy to reload.
Accurate up to about 10 feet and can reach 15. The oily musk clings to everything. Tomato juice does not work well. Hydrogen peroxide, baking soda, and dish soap does.
Grubs, beetle larvae, field mice, bird eggs, berries, and garbage. A skunk rooting in your lawn is eating the grubs that damage the grass.
Skunks are a primary rabies vector in Alabama. Never approach a skunk that's active in daylight or seems disoriented. Contact animal control.

quiz.q: A skunk stamps its front feet before spraying. Why?
choices: It is warning you, because spraying is a last resort
quiz.right: Right. A skunk gives you every chance to leave before it commits.
quiz.wrong: Skunks give fair warning. The foot-stamping, raised tail, and backward shuffle are all saying "please leave so I don't have to spray."

A striped skunk on a mown lawn in side view, its broad white back stripe running to the base of its tail.

species.name: Raccoon
species.body: Raccoons are among the most intelligent and adaptable animals along Five Mile Creek. Their hand-like paws and problem-solving ability make them both fascinating and occasionally frustrating to live alongside.

facts.v: Raccoon paws have exceptional sensitivity. They see with their hands, feeling for crayfish and mussels underwater. The scientific name Procyon lotor means washing pre-dog.
Raccoons can remember solutions to tasks for up to three years and can open complex latches. They regularly defeat "raccoon-proof" garbage cans.
Raccoons can carry rabies, distemper, and roundworm parasites. Don't feed them, don't handle them, and keep your trash secured.
Raccoon tracks are unmistakable. They look like tiny human handprints with five fingers spread wide. Look for them in creek mud.

species.otw: Old-timers hunted raccoons at night with dogs. Coon hunting was one of the major rural pastimes in this area. The dogs would tree the raccoon, and the hunters would follow the sound of the baying.
species.clue: Wet footprints on a flat rock, five tiny fingers, like a small human hand.

species.name: Bobcat
species.body: Bobcats are present along Five Mile Creek but almost never seen. They're roughly twice the size of a house cat, with a bobbed tail, tufted ears, and a spotted coat. Seeing one is genuinely rare, because they see you long before you see them.

facts.v: 15 to 35 pounds, about twice a large house cat. Muscular, low-slung, built for ambush hunting. The bobbed tail is the diagnostic feature.
Rabbits, squirrels, mice, birds, and occasionally fawns. They hunt by stalking and pouncing, not chasing.
Tracks are round with no claw marks (cats retract their claws). Scratch marks on trees and covered scat are territorial signs.
Bobcats are solitary and crepuscular, most active at dawn and dusk. A game camera near a creek crossing is the most reliable way to confirm their presence.

species.otw: Old-timers called them "wildcats" and told stories about their screams at night during mating season, a sound like a person in distress. If you hear it in February or March, that's what it is.
species.clue: A brief glimpse of something tawny and short-tailed moving through undergrowth, already gone.

A bobcat's face close up, pale ruff at the cheeks and dark bars running back from the eyes.

species.name: Groundhog
species.body: Groundhogs (woodchucks) are common along Five Mile Creek's field margins and bottomland edges. They hibernate through the coldest months but are otherwise active and highly visible.

facts.v: Groundhog burrows are important habitat. Foxes, skunks, rabbits, and opossums all use abandoned groundhog dens. One animal's digging creates housing for many others.
Groundhogs genuinely hibernate. Body temperature drops to near freezing and heart rate slows to a few beats per minute. They lose a third of their body weight over winter.
Clover, grasses, dandelion, and garden vegetables. They eat several pounds per day in summer building fat reserves for winter.
A groundhog can excavate more than 700 pounds of dirt for a burrow system. Wildlife biologists actually calculated it. The answer to that old question is: about 700 pounds.

species.clue: A fat, low-slung animal sitting upright at the edge of the field, watching you.

species.name: Eastern Mole
species.ctx: Ridges of pushed-up earth across the yard
species.body: Eastern moles are among the most industrious and least-seen animals here. You'll know they're there by the raised ridges and molehills in your yard. The animal itself lives almost entirely underground.

facts.v: Earthworms, grubs, and beetle larvae. A single mole eats 70 to 100 percent of its body weight daily. They are not eating your plants. They are eating the things that eat your plants.
Moles can dig 18 feet per hour. Their front paws are massive, paddle-shaped, and permanently turned outward, built for nothing but digging.
Mole tunneling aerates soil and mixes organic material deeper into the ground. The lawn damage is cosmetic. The ecological work is real.
Moles are fiercely territorial. Each mole claims its own tunnel system. If you have mole tunnels, you probably have one mole, not an infestation.

species.clue: A raised tunnel of dirt cuts across the lawn in a wavering line.

species.name: Five-lined Skink
species.body: Five-lined skinks are the most common lizard along Five Mile Creek: fast, glossy, and unmistakable with their bright blue tails as juveniles. The blue fades with age but the five cream stripes remain.

facts.v: Juvenile skinks have vivid blue tails. If grabbed by a predator, the tail breaks off and continues wiggling, a decoy while the skink escapes. The tail regrows but never as brightly.

Five cream stripes running head to tail on a dark brown or black body. Juveniles have the electric blue tail. Adult males lose the stripes and turn bronze with reddish-orange heads during breeding season.
Rotting logs, rock piles, old foundations, woodpiles. Anywhere there's shelter and sun nearby. They eat insects, spiders, and small invertebrates.
The broadhead skink is also present, larger, with adult males developing a wide orange red head. Often mistaken for a different species entirely, but it's still a skink.

species.clue: A sleek, striped lizard with a brilliant blue tail sunning on a flat rock.

species.name: Spotted Salamander
species.body: Spotted salamanders are one of the hidden treasures of the Five Mile Creek bottomland: jet black with bright yellow spots, up to 9 inches long, and almost never seen unless you're looking. They spend most of their lives underground.

facts.v: Glossy black body with two rows of bright yellow or orange spots from head to tail. Stout, slow-moving, and docile when found. One of the most beautiful animals in the Alabama forest.
Spotted salamanders migrate to temporary pools (vernal pools) on rainy spring nights to breed. Their egg masses, gelatinous clusters about the size of a softball, are found in shallow water.
Their presence indicates healthy forest with intact leaf litter, moist soil, and seasonal wetlands. They're sensitive to habitat fragmentation and pollution.
Salamanders breathe partly through their skin and absorb chemicals easily. If you find one, look but do not handle, or wet your hands first if you must move it.

species.clue: Lift a damp, rotting log in the bottomland. Something dark and glistening moves slowly underneath.

A spotted salamander on a mossy log, black with yellow spots and its tail curved round.

species.name: Woodpeckers
species.body: These three towns sit in territory that supports an impressive range of woodpeckers. Document every species you see. The red-cockaded woodpecker is a federal priority and any confirmed sighting matters.

facts.v: Pileated, Red-headed, Downy, Hairy, and Yellow-bellied sapsucker are all confirmed in the area. "Yellowhammer" (Northern flicker) is the Alabama state bird.
Federally endangered. Nests only in old-growth longleaf pine with red heart disease. Any sighting should be reported to the Alabama Wildlife Federation.
The largest woodpecker in North America at nearly 20 inches. Its rectangular excavations in dead trees are distinctive. Sounds like a jungle bird, a loud laughing call.
The northern flicker is Alabama's state bird. Named for the yellow-shafted underside of its wings. More often seen on the ground than in trees, feeding on ants.

species.otw: Woodpecker holes are real estate in the forest. Screech owls, wood ducks, flying squirrels, and a dozen other species move into abandoned woodpecker cavities. One bird's work feeds an entire community.

quiz.q: This part of Jefferson County may have one of the rarest woodpeckers in North America. Which one?
quiz.right: Correct, and it is a big deal if confirmed here.
quiz.wrong: The red-cockaded woodpecker is the one to watch for. It is federally endangered and present in parts of north Alabama.

A red headed woodpecker at the entrance to a cavity in a dead trunk.
A deep oval hole cut into a standing dead tree, the kind a pileated woodpecker leaves.

species.name: Chicken Hawk
species.body: The red-tailed hawk is the large buteo you'll see circling over Five Mile Creek's fields and forest edges. Its call is the one Hollywood uses for every eagle in every movie, that piercing scream.

facts.v: The red-tailed hawk's call is used in virtually every Hollywood movie and TV show for any bird of prey, including bald eagles, which actually sound like seagulls.
Field mice, voles, rabbits, squirrels, and occasional small birds. One red-tail can significantly reduce rodent pressure on a property.
Red-tails prefer high, open perches with a view: fence posts, dead trees, power poles. Once you know what to look for, you'll see them everywhere.
The Cooper's hawk, also called a chicken hawk, actually does take chickens and birds. It's a fast, agile accipiter that hunts through forest, not the circling buteo.

species.otw: Old-timers with chicken flocks had a complicated relationship with hawks. The big ones circling high were mostly harmless to full grown chickens. It is the small fast ones in the trees that took birds.
species.lookalike: Often called a chicken hawk. Locally that usually means a red-tailed hawk, though broad-winged hawks can confuse people in migration.
species.local: Most often noticed circling above meadow edges and utility clearings, especially late afternoon.

quiz.q: "Chicken hawk" is a local name for which bird?
quiz.right: Right. The red-tailed hawk is the bird most people around here call a chicken hawk.
quiz.wrong: The most common "chicken hawk" people see is actually the red-tailed hawk, the one circling in thermals over fields.

photos.alt: A red-tailed hawk perched on top of a utility pole above the wires, watching the ground.
A red-tailed hawk soaring against a pale sky, seen from below with its tail fanned.

species.name: Owls
species.body: Multiple owl species work the Five Mile Creek corridor at night. The barred owl is the most commonly heard, the great horned owl is the apex predator, and the tiny screech owl might be living in a woodpecker hole in your yard right now.

facts.v: The who cooks for you call. Medium-large, brown-eyed, no ear tufts. Common along wooded creeks. Sometimes calls in full daylight, especially on overcast days.
The largest owl in the area, with ear tufts, yellow eyes, and a deep hoo hoo hoooo call. Will take prey as large as skunks and small cats. Nests in January.
Tiny enough to fit in a coffee mug. Makes a descending whinny, not a screech. Lives in tree cavities. Put up a nest box and you might get one in your yard.
Owls swallow prey whole and regurgitate pellets of bone and fur. Finding pellets under a large tree is proof an owl is roosting above. Dissecting them is a biology lesson.

quiz.q: You hear a deep "who-cooks-for-you, who-cooks-for-you-ALL" at night. Which owl?
quiz.right: Right. That eight syllable call is the barred owl's signature.
quiz.wrong: That is the barred owl, the most vocal owl in the eastern woods. The who cooks for you call is unmistakable once you know it.

photos.alt: A barred owl perched on a wire against a pale sky, round headed with dark eyes and barred brown and white plumage.
A great horned owl on a branch against a tree trunk, ear tufts up and body streaked grey and brown.
A barred owl sitting among green leaves on a low branch.

species.name: Bats
species.body: Several bat species work the Five Mile Creek corridor at dusk, including big brown bats, evening bats, and red bats. They emerge at twilight and spend the night consuming enormous quantities of insects.

facts.v: A single bat can eat 1,000+ mosquitoes per night, along with moths, beetles, and other flying insects. A colony near your house is a gift, not a problem.
A devastating fungal disease has killed millions of bats across eastern North America. Alabama populations have been affected. Healthy bat colonies are more important than ever.
Properly placed bat houses can attract colonies. Mount them 12 to 15 feet high on a pole or building, facing south or southeast for morning sun.
Bats can carry rabies, but less than 1% do. Never handle a bat with bare hands. If you find a grounded bat, call animal control.

quiz.q: A single bat can eat how many mosquitoes in one night?
quiz.right: Right. A thousand mosquitoes in a single night. Bats are the night shift for pest control.
quiz.wrong: A single bat can consume over 1,000 mosquitoes in one night. They are one of the most effective insect controllers in the ecosystem.

photos.alt: A bat clinging to a rough stone wall with its wings folded and one long ear turned forward.
A bat held open in gloved hands, its wing membranes stretched between long finger bones.
A small bat hanging against a sandy coloured wall, wrapped in its own wings.

species.name: Periodical Cicada
species.body: Periodical cicadas spend 13 years underground as nymphs feeding on tree roots, then emerge all at once in enormous numbers. This whole stretch of the creek sits in Brood XIX territory, the Great Southern Brood.

facts.v: A chorus of periodical cicadas can reach 100 decibels, as loud as a motorcycle. Each male vibrates a membrane called a tymbal.
13 years underground, five molts. They emerge, mate, lay eggs, and die within weeks. The eggs hatch, nymphs drop to ground, cycle starts again.
The Great Southern Brood covers much of the South including north Alabama. Last emerged in 2024, a historic year when Brood XIII and XIX emerged simultaneously for the first time since 1803.
Dead branches from egg-laying fertilize soil when they fall. The emergence aerates soil. Cicadas are good for the land. They just sound like the apocalypse.

species.otw: Old-timers said a heavy cicada year meant a good acorn crop to follow, and a good acorn crop meant fat squirrels come fall.

quiz.q: Periodical cicadas in Alabama emerge on a 13-year cycle. What are they doing when they make that noise?
quiz.right: Right. Every one of those is a male trying to find a mate.
quiz.wrong: That deafening chorus is all males singing for females, one of the loudest sounds in nature.

A periodical cicada gripping bark, seen from above, its orange wing veins folded along its back.

species.name: Turkey Vulture
species.body: Turkey vultures are the clean-up crew of the Five Mile Creek corridor. They soar on thermals with a distinctive wobbling, V-shaped wing profile, and they perform an essential ecological function: removing carrion before it becomes a disease vector.

facts.v: Turkey vultures can detect ethyl mercaptan, the gas released by decomposition, from more than a mile away. Gas companies add this same chemical to natural gas so humans can smell leaks.
Large, dark bird soaring with wings in a shallow V (dihedral). Wobbly, teetering flight. Red, featherless head in adults. Often mistaken for eagles at a distance.
They urinate on their own legs to kill bacteria picked up from carrion, a process called urohydrosis. It also cools them. Disgusting and brilliant.
Black vultures are also present. Shorter, broader wings held flat. They find food by following turkey vultures, not by smell. More aggressive at carcasses.

quiz.q: Turkey vultures hold their wings in a distinctive V-shape while soaring. How do they find food?
choices: Primarily by smell, one of the few birds that can
quiz.right: Right. Turkey vultures are one of the very few birds with a strong sense of smell.
quiz.wrong: Turkey vultures hunt primarily by smell. They can detect the gas from decomposition from miles away. One of the few bird species with this ability.

species.name: Painted Turtle
species.body: Painted turtles and sliders are the turtles you see basking on logs in every pond and slow stretch of Five Mile Creek. They stack up in rows, slide into the water at the slightest disturbance, and climb right back up five minutes later.

facts.v: Turtles bask to regulate body temperature and to dry out their shells, which prevents algae and parasites from taking hold. It's not laziness, it's maintenance.
Red-eared sliders and painted turtles are most common. Snapping turtles are also present but stay in the water. Softshell turtles occasionally show up in sandy-bottomed areas.
Aquatic plants, insects, small fish, and carrion. They're omnivorous scavengers that help keep the water clean.
Red-eared sliders sold as pets and released into the wild are an invasive problem in many waterways. Don't release pet turtles.

species.name: Roly-Poly
species.body: The roly-poly (pillbug or woodlouse) is not actually an insect. It is a crustacean, more closely related to crayfish and shrimp than to any bug. It's the only crustacean fully adapted to life on land.

facts.v: Roly-polies breathe through gills, need moist environments, and are more closely related to crayfish than to any insect. One of evolution's more surprising moves.
They decompose dead plant material, cycling nutrients back into the soil. Critical to the decomposer community that keeps the bottomland functioning.
Rolling into a perfect sphere exposes only the armored back. It works against most small predators, though birds and toads learn to wait for them to unroll.
The roly-poly may be the most important gateway species in natural history, the creature that makes kids curious about what else is living under rocks. Don't underestimate it.

species.clue: Lift a rock near the damp bank. Grey armored things curl into balls.

species.name: Field Mouse
species.ctx: In the grass at the bank edge
species.body: Field mice (white-footed mice and deer mice) are the most numerous mammals along Five Mile Creek, and the foundation of the food web that feeds foxes, coyotes, hawks, owls, and snakes.

facts.v: Field mice convert seeds, berries, and insects into protein for every predator in the watershed. Without them, the food chain above collapses.
In a good year, mouse populations can explode dramatically. A high mouse year is followed by a good year for hawks, owls, foxes, and coyotes. The system self-regulates.
White-footed mice can carry hantavirus. Don't handle live or dead mice, and ventilate before cleaning spaces where mice have nested.
White-footed mice cache thousands of seeds and forget many of them. A significant portion of the forest regenerates from mice's forgotten food stores.

species.clue: A tiny rustle in the grass at the creek bank. Something very small is moving.

species.name: Wildflowers
species.ctx: Along the trail and field edges
species.body: The fields and forest edges along the creek host a rotating display of native wildflowers from early spring through fall. They are not just pretty. They are the foundation of the pollinator food web that supports everything above them.

facts.v: Trillium, bloodroot, hepatica, and Virginia bluebells bloom before the canopy fills in, using the brief window of direct sunlight on the forest floor. April is prime time.
Black-eyed Susan, bee balm, ironweed, and Joe-Pye weed dominate the sunny meadows and road edges from June through August.
The wild passion flower (Passiflora incarnata, called maypop) grows along fences and field edges. Its elaborate purple flower is one of the most striking native blooms. The fruit is edible when ripe.
Native wildflowers support native bees, butterflies, and moths that commercial crops depend on for pollination. Every patch of wildflowers is doing economic work.

species.clue: A patch of color at the sunny edge of the trail catches your eye.

species.name: Wild Passion Flower
species.ctx: Climbing a fence at the field edge
species.body: The wild passion flower, called maypop locally because the hollow fruit may pop when you step on it, produces one of the most architecturally complex flowers of any plant in North America. It's native here and it's spectacular.

facts.v: Purple filaments radiating from a central column in a geometric pattern. Spanish missionaries saw in it symbols of the Passion of Christ: the filaments as the crown of thorns, the five anthers as the five wounds.
The maypop fruit is edible when ripe (yellow-green, slightly soft). The pulp inside tastes tropical, related to commercial passion fruit but milder. Makes good jelly.
The Gulf fritillary butterfly lays its eggs exclusively on passion flower vines. The caterpillars eat the leaves and develop toxic compounds from the plant that make them unpalatable to birds.
Passionflower has documented mild sedative and anxiolytic properties and is used in herbal medicine. The dried leaves make a tea. Research supports its calming effects.

species.clue: An intricate purple and white flower unlike anything else, climbing a wire fence.

photos.alt: A wild passion flower open on the ground beside its vine, purple and white filaments radiating from a central column.

species.name: Canada Geese
species.body: Canada geese migrate through these three towns in fall and winter, using Five Mile Creek as a rest stop. Seeing a big flock on the water is one of the genuine spectacles of the season.

facts.v: Peak movement through north Alabama is October through December. They follow creek corridors south.
Open water and nearby fields or grassy areas for feeding. Five Mile Creek bottomland provides both.
The high and low honking duet, two birds, two tones, calling back and forth. Once you know it, you'll hear them flying over at night.
Canada geese are a prized waterfowl in Alabama. Season runs October through January. Check ADCNR for current dates and bag limits.

species.otw: Old-timers watched geese flights to predict weather. A flock flying fast and low usually meant a front was coming. Flying high and slow meant clear skies ahead. Not science, but not wrong either.
species.clue: A large flock of birds drops out of the sky onto Five Mile Creek.

photos.alt: Three Canada geese walking single file across wet pavement, black necked with white cheek patches.

A scattered flock of Canada geese grazing across a mown field.

species.name: Wild Turkey
species.body: Wild turkeys were nearly extinct in Alabama by the early 1900s due to overhunting and habitat loss. Conservation efforts brought them back, and they're now common along Five Mile Creek's bottomland and forest edges.

facts.v: Alabama's wild turkey population recovered from near-zero to over 400,000 birds through one of the most successful wildlife restoration programs in American history.
Wild turkeys are far more intelligent and wary than their domestic cousins. They have excellent color vision, can run 25 mph, and fly short distances at up to 55 mph.
Alabama's spring turkey season is one of the most popular hunting seasons in the state. Calling a gobbler into range requires genuine skill and patience.
Turkeys roost in trees at night, usually large oaks or pines near water. They fly up at dusk and fly down at dawn. Finding a roost tree is key to hunting them.

quiz.q: A male wild turkey "gobbles" primarily to:
quiz.right: Right. The gobble is a mating call. Everything about a tom in spring is about attracting hens.
quiz.wrong: The gobble is a mating call. The tom is advertising himself to every hen within hearing distance. It also announces his position to rival males.

photos.alt: A hen turkey standing in tall green grass beside a wire fence with her head up.
A wild turkey's blue and white head and neck above green brush.
A wild turkey out in an open field in front of a treeline.

species.name: Kudzu
species.body: Kudzu was introduced as an ornamental and for erosion control. It has no natural predators in North America, grows up to a foot per day in summer, and covers everything that doesn't move regularly.

facts.v: Repeated cutting at ground level over 2 to 3 seasons exhausts the root. Goats are surprisingly effective. Herbicide works but must stay away from the water.
Often the same native hardwoods that were there before. Kudzu shades but doesn't always kill them. Clearing reveals what's underneath.
Chinese privet is equally aggressive along Five Mile Creek. It leaves out earlier, crowds out native seedlings, and birds spread its berries everywhere.
Every acre cleared on the Five Mile Creek bank is an acre returning to bottomland forest, which filters water, prevents erosion, and supports wildlife.

species.otw: The old clearing tradition: work in the same place every year, a little more each time. The land remembers what it was supposed to be. You're just helping it get back there.

quiz.q: Kudzu can grow how fast in Alabama summer conditions?
choices: Up to a foot per day
It grows slowly but just keeps spreading
quiz.right: A foot per day. That's not a plant, that's a siege.
quiz.wrong: A foot per day in peak summer. By the end of August it has covered everything it started on in June.

species.name: Poison Ivy
species.body: Poison ivy grows enthusiastically along Five Mile Creek. Learn to identify it in every season. The leafless winter vine is the sneakiest.

facts.v: Three leaflets, the middle one on a longer stalk. Glossy when young, can be red in spring and fall. Grows as ground cover, shrub, or large vine on trees.
Poison ivy vines on trees develop a distinctive hairy appearance from aerial rootlets, the fuzzy rope vine. Do not touch it in any season.
The bare stems and roots in winter still carry urushiol. People who burn brush in winter and inhale the smoke can develop severe internal reactions. That is a medical emergency.
Wash with soap and cold water immediately after exposure. The oil takes 10 to 30 minutes to bond to skin, so quick washing can prevent or reduce the rash.

species.otw: Old-timers said if you ate a small poison ivy leaf every spring you'd build immunity. This is dangerous advice, because some people are extremely sensitive. The actual traditional remedy was jewel weed, also called touch-me-not, which grows near poison ivy and whose juice soothes the rash.

quiz.q: The saying is "leaves of three, let it be." When along Five Mile Creek is poison ivy most dangerous to touch?
choices: Only in summer when the leaves are fully green
All year, including winter when it is leafless
Only when the leaves turn red in fall
Only when it's flowering in spring
quiz.right: Correct. The urushiol oil is present year round, including on bare winter stems.
quiz.wrong: All year round. The urushiol oil that causes the rash is in the stems, roots, and berries, not just the leaves.

A poison ivy vine on a tree trunk, thick with the reddish brown aerial rootlets that give it the look of a fuzzy rope.

species.name: Beaver
species.ctx: At the edge of still water
species.body: Beavers are watershed engineers. Where they work, water slows, sediment settles out, and a whole new wet place appears. A beaver pond is not just a puddle. It is a different habitat built by teeth and patience.

facts.v: Fresh-cut saplings with a sharpened-pencil point, muddy slides, peeled bark, and quiet ponding water are the giveaway signs.
Beaver ponds hold water on the land, trap silt before it reaches the creek, and create habitat for frogs, dragonflies, herons, and turtles.
Beavers do most of their work at dusk and through the night. You usually see the evidence before you see the animal.

species.otw: If the branch that used to run clear is backing up and spreading out, do not guess. Walk the edge. A beaver has likely made itself part of the conversation.
species.clue: Freshly gnawed sticks and a slick mud slide cut into the bank.

photos.alt: A sapling cut off at an angle beside the creek, the stump sharpened to a point by beaver teeth.
A beaver swimming in still water behind a fence line with only its back and head above the surface.

species.name: Black-eyed Susan
species.ctx: At the sunny edge of the field
species.body: Black-eyed Susan is one of the signature flowers of an Alabama roadside meadow: bright, tough, and busy with bees. It is not just decoration. It is food and structure for pollinators when summer gets hard and hot.

facts.v: Native bees, butterflies, and small beetles all work these flowers. A patch in bloom is a feeding station.
After bloom, the dark seed heads feed goldfinches and other small birds into fall.
It handles heat, disturbed ground, and poor soils better than many showier flowers. That is part of why it belongs here.

species.otw: If you want to know whether a field still has some life in it, stand still by the black-eyed Susans and count what lands there.
species.clue: A stand of yellow flowers holds the heat of the afternoon.

species.name: Blue Jay
species.body: Blue jays are the town criers of the woods. Sharp-eyed, noisy, and smarter than people give them credit for, they warn everything around them when a hawk, snake, cat, or stranger moves through.

facts.v: When blue jays start scolding, other birds pay attention. They are often the first to announce that a predator is nearby.
Blue jays carry and hide acorns. They forget some of them, which means they accidentally plant trees.
They can imitate hawk calls. Sometimes they mean it as a warning; sometimes they seem to enjoy stirring things up.

species.otw: A blue jay can save you time. If it is raising Cain in one direction, that is where the story is.
species.clue: A loud blue bird raises a fuss before you ever spot it.

species.name: Bullfrog
species.ctx: On the still edge after dark
species.body: Bullfrogs own the summer night in Alabama. Bigger than green frogs, heavier-voiced, and fond of still edges and quiet water, they are hunters from the tadpole stage on.

facts.v: Insects, crayfish, fish, other frogs, and anything else they can overpower. A big bullfrog is not delicate about what counts as supper.
Bullfrog tadpoles may stay in the water more than one year before changing into frogs.
Warm, wet evenings from late spring through midsummer are when the chorus is strongest.

species.otw: Lantern light and a still bank used to be enough for frog gigging. If the night feels heavy and warm, listen first and move second.

quiz.q: When people say a bullfrog sounds like a jug of rum, what call are they talking about?
quiz.right: Right. That deep jug-o-rum is the bullfrog.
quiz.wrong: The bullfrog is the deep one, the classic jug-o-rum rolling out over still water.

A bullfrog in shallow brown water with only its head and shoulders showing.

species.name: Northern Cardinal
species.ctx: In the hedge and low limbs
species.body: The cardinal is one of the few birds that feels like it belongs to every season at once. Bright in winter, vocal in spring, and loyal to edges, thickets, and yards, it bridges the wild and the tended.

facts.v: Unlike many songbirds, female cardinals sing too. Mated pairs often answer each other.
Cardinals like the in-between places: hedges, fence lines, brushy edges, and open understory.
That red against gray woods is why people remember them, but they are just as much a summer bird as a winter one.

species.otw: When the woods look empty, a cardinal will often prove they are not.
species.clue: A red flash lands in the privet and disappears.

photos.alt: A male northern cardinal on a patio, bright red with a black face and a raised crest.
A young cardinal perched on a bare branch, brown bodied with the beginnings of a crest.
A cardinal at the wing mirror of a car, going after its own reflection.

species.name: Hickory Tussock Moth Caterpillar
species.ctx: On a leaf at hand height
species.body: The Hickory Tussock Moth caterpillar is beautiful and absolutely not for handling. Those pale hairs can cause an itchy rash and a lesson you would rather skip.

facts.v: Its barbed hairs can break in the skin and cause stinging, redness, and itching in sensitive people.
Hickory, walnut, pecan, ash, and elm are all on the menu. They are usually a brief defoliator, not a lasting disaster.
Admire hairy caterpillars with your eyes first. Bare fingers are not the tool for this kind of beauty.

species.otw: Around here, if a caterpillar looks especially soft, assume the Lord gave it that look for its own protection, not your comfort.
species.clue: A shaggy white caterpillar looks soft enough to touch. Don't.

species.name: Channel Catfish
species.ctx: In a deep bend after rain
species.body: Channel catfish haunt deeper holes, cut banks, and slow runs where the creek settles down. They are working fish: whiskered, patient, and built for water that is not perfectly clear.

facts.v: Cut bait, chicken liver, nightcrawlers, or something oily that puts a smell line in the water.
Outside bends, deeper holes below riffles, and any cover that breaks current are worth your time.
Watch the sharp pectoral and dorsal spines. A small catfish can stick you worse than a big one if you get careless.

species.otw: If the creek has color after a rain, that is catfish weather. Let the bait sit where the current slackens and wait longer than you want to.

quiz.q: In stained or muddy water, what does a channel catfish rely on most to find food?
choices: Taste and smell through barbels and skin
quiz.right: Exactly. Catfish live by taste and smell in dirty water.
quiz.wrong: Catfish are built for murky water. They use taste and smell through their barbels and skin more than sight.

species.name: Cattails
species.body: Cattails mark wet ground the way a church steeple marks a town. Where they stand, water has a say. They anchor soft edges, slow runoff, and provide cover for frogs, birds, insects, and muskrats where those still exist.

facts.v: A stand of cattails means the soil stays wet enough for roots to live in waterlogged ground.
Red-winged blackbirds, dragonflies, frogs, and countless insects use cattail stands for cover and nesting.
People have used cattails for mats, stuffing, tinder, and food parts in the right season. A useful plant if you know it well.

species.otw: If you see cattails, stop pretending it is dry ground just because grass is growing there.
species.clue: Tall blades and brown seed heads stand where the ground turns to muck.

species.name: Chicken Snake
species.ctx: On a fence or in the rafters
species.body: The chicken snake, the local name for a black rat snake, is long, calm compared with most snakes, and excellent at climbing. It belongs around barns, sheds, and brushy edges because that is where the rodents are.

facts.v: It may bluff, vibrate its tail, and act offended, but it is not a venomous snake.
Rat snakes can climb rough bark, walls, rafters, and almost anything with a little purchase.
Mice, rats, young birds, and eggs are all on the menu. In a feed room, that is useful work.

species.otw: A barn with one chicken snake usually has fewer mice than a barn without one.

quiz.q: Why did people around here tolerate chicken snakes even when they raided eggs now and then?
quiz.right: Right. A good rat snake earns its keep by eating rodents.
quiz.wrong: The main reason was simple: rat snakes kill rats and mice, which saves feed, eggs, and trouble.

species.name: Eastern Chipmunk
species.ctx: Near a rock pile in the woods
species.body: Chipmunks are quick little edge-runners of the woods, more often heard chipping than properly seen. They love rock piles, roots, old foundations, and any place that gives them both seed and cover.

facts.v: Chipmunks dig extensive burrows with storage chambers, sleeping rooms, and several entrances they keep surprisingly tidy.
Nuts, seeds, berries, acorns, and fungi all get carried underground for later.
They spend much more time on the ground and vanish into holes instead of heading for the canopy.

species.otw: If you find a quiet stone pile and sit long enough, the chipmunk will often forgive your presence before most bigger animals do.
species.clue: A striped little body shoots from log to stump and freezes.

species.name: Copperhead
species.ctx: Still as leaf litter on the trail edge
species.body: Copperheads are the venomous snake most people around here are most likely to meet in leaf litter, brushy edges, wood piles, and warm rocks. Their best defense is staying still, which is also why boots and attention matter.

facts.v: A copperhead disappears into dead leaves better than most people expect. That is why so many encounters happen at close range.
Edges, cover, brush piles, old boards, and sunny spots near shelter. They do not need a swamp to be present.
Watch where you step, do not put hands where you cannot see, and wear boots or gaiters during warm months.

species.otw: Around old houses and wood piles, assume a copperhead could be under the board you are about to move.

quiz.q: What is the safest rule when you spot a snake you are not fully sure about?
choices: Get closer for a better look
Back off and leave it alone
Try to pin its head with a stick
quiz.right: Exactly. Distance is the right answer every time.
quiz.wrong: The safest, smartest move is to back off and leave it alone. No close inspection is required.

photos.alt: A copperhead coiled on wet leaves, tan with dark chestnut crossbands that are narrow across the back and wide down the sides.

species.name: Cottonmouth
species.body: Cottonmouths are real, but they are not under every rock in the creek. Give slow, swampy margins the respect they deserve, and do not turn every harmless water snake into a moccasin out of habit.

facts.v: Swamps, oxbows, sloughs, beaver ponds, and flooded backwaters are much more their style than lively moving water.
When threatened they may coil, hold ground, and flash the pale mouth that gave them their common name.
If you are not certain, do not test your certainty with your hands. Step back and leave it be.

species.otw: People around here called every water snake a moccasin for generations. The swamp deserves caution, but accuracy matters too.
species.lookalike: The northern water snake gets killed for this one constantly. A cottonmouth has a blocky head and swims with its body riding high. When you cannot tell, you do not need to.

quiz.q: Along the Five Mile Creek watershed, where are you more likely to meet a true cottonmouth?
choices: In fast riffles over clean rock
In still, swampy water with cover
quiz.right: Right. Cottonmouths fit still, swampy water better than fast creek water.
quiz.wrong: Cottonmouths are much more at home in still, swampy water than in a fast clean riffle.

species.name: American Crow
species.body: Crows are among the smartest birds in the watershed. They notice people, patterns, tools, predators, and opportunity. If a crow is making a scene, it usually has a reason.

facts.v: Crows remember faces, learn routines, and can work out surprisingly complicated food problems.
They will harass owls, hawks, and even eagles in groups when they think a threat is too close.
Young from prior years often help parents feed a new nest. Crow society is more organized than it first appears.

species.otw: A crow seldom wastes a commotion. If several are carrying on in one place, look there.
species.clue: A black bird calls from high up like it has something to say about all of this.

photos.alt: An American crow walking across mown grass, entirely black including its bill and legs.

species.name: Funeral Bells
species.ctx: On a damp log after rain
species.body: Funeral bells are the reason experienced foragers speak carefully about little brown mushrooms. Unremarkable at first glance, growing on wood like several edible species, and loaded with the same amatoxins that make death cap mushrooms infamous.

facts.v: These are not "upset your stomach" mushrooms. They can destroy the liver and kill.
They overlap visually with harmless and edible wood-growing mushrooms enough to punish carelessness.
If you are not fully certain on a mushroom, it is not food. Full stop.

species.otw: The old rule still holds: little brown mushrooms will humble a proud person in a hurry.
species.lookalike: Every year somebody eats a small brown mushroom they were almost sure about. If you are not fully confident, do not eat any little brown mushroom.

quiz.q: Why is a small brown mushroom on wood worth extra caution?
choices: Some small brown mushrooms are lethally poisonous
They are too bitter to eat
quiz.right: Right. Small brown mushrooms can be some of the most dangerous things in the woods.
quiz.wrong: That is the danger. Tiny brown mushrooms are not harmless by default. Some, like funeral bells, can be lethal.

species.name: Goldenrod
species.body: Goldenrod is one of the great late season plants of the South, a pollinator lifeline when much of the field is tired and drying down. If the meadow hums in September, goldenrod is usually part of the reason.

facts.v: Bees, wasps, butterflies, flies, and beetles all work goldenrod hard in late summer and early fall.
People blame goldenrod for hay fever because it blooms when ragweed does. Ragweed is the real sneeze-maker; goldenrod pollen is heavier and insect-carried.
This is one of the important last big nectar sources before cold weather closes the year down.

species.otw: When goldenrod blooms, the field is not done. It is finishing strong.
species.clue: Tall yellow sprays lean into late summer light.

species.name: Tomato Hornworm
species.ctx: On the garden row at dusk
species.body: Tomato hornworms are masters of not being seen until the damage is obvious. Big, green, and leaf-colored, they can strip a tomato plant fast if you do not catch them early.

facts.v: Dark droppings on lower leaves or the ground are often easier to spot than the caterpillar itself.
If a hornworm is covered with white cocoons, leave it. Parasitic wasps have already claimed it and are doing you a favor.
This caterpillar becomes a large sphinx moth, one of the strong flying pollinating moths of summer nights.

species.otw: If the tomatoes suddenly look chewed and you cannot find the thief, stand still at eye level and follow the damage upward.
species.clue: The tomato plant looks thinner than it did yesterday. Look closely.

species.name: Ironweed
species.ctx: Standing tall in the wet meadow
species.body: Ironweed is one of those plants that makes a meadow feel honest. Tall, purple, late, and loaded with pollinators, it tells you the season is turning even while the heat is still hanging on.

facts.v: Giant ironweed thrives in moist meadows, ditches, and low ground that stays richer than the dry upland.
Swallowtails, monarchs, skippers, bees, and wasps all use it.
When ironweed is up, you are looking at a field that has at least some structure left in it.

species.otw: A meadow with ironweed still has backbone.
species.clue: A purple stand rises above the rest of the meadow like a banner.

Ironweed in flower at the edge of a field, purple heads on tall stems above green leaves.

species.name: Belted Kingfisher
species.ctx: On a branch over the creek
species.body: The belted kingfisher is one of the true creek birds: loud, top heavy, blue gray, and all business. When you hear that dry rattling call along the water, the creek still has somebody working it.

facts.v: Kingfishers perch, hover, or patrol, then dive headfirst into the creek for small fish and crayfish.
They tunnel into vertical dirt banks to nest, which means a hard clean cut bank can be valuable habitat.
The bridge coming into town is exactly the kind of place a kingfisher likes: a clear view, water below, and a perch with authority.

species.otw: Watch where the kingfisher dives. That is information.
species.clue: A rattling call zips down the creek before you find the bird.

species.name: Kingsnake
species.ctx: Crossing warm ground after a cool night
species.body: Kingsnakes are handsome, clean-patterned, and remarkably effective predators. They are not venomous, but they are well-equipped for taking down rodents and sometimes other snakes much bigger than you would expect.

facts.v: Kingsnakes overpower prey by coiling and squeezing, then swallowing it whole.
They are famous for eating other snakes, which is part of how they got the name.
A kingsnake on your place is usually helping more than hurting.

species.otw: If you have feed, you have mice. If you have mice, a kingsnake is worth more than most people know.
species.lookalike: Dark and glossy like a chicken snake, but shorter, heavier, and chain marked. Both are worth having around.

quiz.q: Why have farmers and old-timers long liked kingsnakes around barns and edges?
choices: They keep rodents and other snakes in check
quiz.right: Exactly. Kingsnakes do useful work where feed and rodents meet.
quiz.wrong: The respect comes from usefulness. Kingsnakes eat rodents and other snakes, including venomous ones when the chance comes.
