species.name: Northern Mockingbird
species.ctx: On the wire over the yard
species.body: Mockingbirds stitch the sounds of a place together. Alarm notes, borrowed phrases, repeats, attitude, and stamina. One good mockingbird can make the whole yard sound more crowded than it is.

facts.v: Mockingbirds borrow from other birds and from whatever sounds have impressed them enough to keep.
During nesting season they defend space fiercely and will dive people, cats, hawks, and anything else that seems rude.
Unmated males and city birds often sing at night under lights.

species.otw: If one bird sounds like six, it is probably a mockingbird showing off.
species.clue: One bird keeps changing the song every few seconds.

species.name: Pokeweed
species.ctx: In disturbed ground by the edge
species.body: Pokeweed is one of the great Southern contradiction plants: beautiful, useful to wildlife, traditionally eaten when very young and correctly prepared, and dangerous enough to make fools of the careless.

facts.v: Only the very young spring shoots have been traditionally cooked as food, and only after repeated boiling with the water discarded. Getting casual with poke is a mistake.
The dark berries feed birds in late season, which is why poke pops up so often under fence lines and trees.
Roots, mature stems, and seeds are more dangerous. Treat the whole plant with respect.

species.otw: Your elders were not wrong about poke salad, but they also did not skip the hard part. Knowledge is what makes the difference.
species.clue: A strong-stemmed plant rises fast where the ground has been turned or neglected.

species.name: Eastern Cottontail
species.ctx: At the edge where grass meets brush
species.body: Rabbits belong to the edge, not deep woods, not open field, but that in-between country where cover and food sit side by side. When brushy edges disappear, rabbits usually go with them.

facts.v: Brush piles, briars, field margins, and young growth are rabbit country.
Foxes, hawks, coyotes, bobcats, and owls all know rabbit country too.
A rabbit trusts stillness before speed. Many people walk past one before the ears give it away.

species.otw: A place with rabbits still has some cover in it somewhere, even if the field looks open at first glance.
species.clue: Something still and brown becomes obvious only when it moves.

photos.alt: An eastern cottontail sitting on mown grass at the edge of a lawn with woods behind it.
A cottontail in tall green grass with its ears up, watching.
A rabbit on a dirt path at the edge of brush.

species.name: Snapping Turtle
species.ctx: In the mud line where water gets quiet
species.body: Snapping turtles are old-country animals: armored, patient, and not interested in small talk. In the water they usually mind their business. Out of the water they remind you quickly that they are not a box turtle.

facts.v: Give a snapping turtle space. Do not try to pick one up unless you truly know what you are doing.
They are most defensive on land because that is where they feel most exposed.
Snappers eat living prey, carrion, and almost anything animal-rich they can manage. They help clean things up.

species.otw: Never lift a snapping turtle by the tail. You can hurt the turtle and teach yourself a bad lesson at the same time.
species.clue: A dark shell and ancient face appear where the water clouds up.

photos.alt: A snapping turtle walking across gravel in side view, rough shelled with a long thick tail and a heavy hooked beak.
A large snapping turtle on sand facing the camera, its head drawn back over massive front legs.

species.name: Gray Squirrel
species.body: Gray squirrels are part clown, part forester, part prey animal, and part acorn accountant. They shape the woods more than people credit them for because every buried nut is a decision about tomorrow.

facts.v: Squirrels bury acorns, hickory nuts, and walnuts all over the woods. Many of those become future trees.
That leafy ball high in the fork is a squirrel nest, called a drey.
Cut hickory shells, chewed pine cones, and scattered nut chips under a tree mean squirrels have been working above you.

species.otw: If you want to know where the mast crop is strongest, look under the tree for shells before you look up for squirrels.
species.clue: A bark shower falls before the squirrel comes into view.

photos.alt: A grey squirrel sitting upright on its haunches in green grass with its tail curled up behind it.
A grey squirrel on a branch among brown oak leaves, feeding.
A squirrel out on a thin branch in a pine, gripping with all four feet.

species.name: Tick
species.ctx: Waiting at knee height in the grass
species.body: Ticks are not rare events in this country. They are part of warm-weather life wherever grass, edges, brush, deer, mice, and people overlap. That means prevention is a habit, not a mood.

facts.v: Ticks climb stems and hold out front legs, waiting to grab passing fur, fabric, or skin.
Use fine tweezers, grab close to the skin, and pull steadily. Then wash the area and your hands.
Light pants, tucked socks, and a full body check after the walk beat wishful thinking every time.

species.otw: If you walked the tall grass, check before you sit down on the couch.

quiz.q: After walking grass or brush in warm weather, what is the smartest next move?
choices: Do a tick check as soon as you get in
Cover the bite in nail polish
quiz.right: Exactly. The sooner you find them, the better.
quiz.wrong: Do the tick check early. Fast removal matters more than old folk remedies.

species.name: Wisteria
species.ctx: Climbing over what it can get hold of
species.body: Wisteria is beautiful enough to get forgiven too easily. The showy blooms are real, but so is the strangling, shading, and weight it puts on trees and edges when it gets loose.

facts.v: The heavy, aggressive blankets people complain about are often nonnative wisterias rather than the more restrained native species.
Large vines add real weight and shade, pulling branches down and smothering understory growth.
Control usually means cutting stems near the base and staying after resprouts, not just pulling the pretty flowers.

species.otw: A vine can be handsome and still be a problem. Wisteria is proof.
species.clue: Purple hanging blooms make a vine look more innocent than it is.
